newsitem.title: USA: Soros challenges venture capitalists on de-mining.
newsitem.headline: Soros challenges venture capitalists on de-mining.

text.p: Billionaire financier George Soros on Tuesday urged the World Bank and venture capitalists to help fund new technologies for landmine detection and clearance.

Soros, at a conference on mine neutralization and removal techniques, said the multi-billion-dollar cost of cleaning up the estimated 110 million mines in 68 countries was too great to be undertaken by private groups, including his charitable foundations.

"Ultimately it must be a responsibility of governments and international organizations, because no one else can muster the necessary resources," said Soros, who manages the Quantum Fund, possibly the world's largest hedge fund, a type of private investment partnership.
Despite what he called the need for technology developers to rely on governmental funding for much of their research and development, Soros cited an opportunity for private venture capital funders.

"It frankly surprises me that venture capitalists have not already entered this field," he told the forum organized by Defense Week and White House Weekly. "The ultimate market is there; NATO and other military forces are desperate for better mine detection equipment."

"Let me be quite plain: the entrepreneur who comes up with effective improvements in detection and clearance stands to make money, and the venture capitalist who fund it stands to do the same," Soros said.
He called on the World Bank to fund mine clearance as well as to study the economics of all aspects of landmines, from production and export to their toll on development.

Through his charitable network of Soros Foundations, the financier said he would put up at least $4 million over the next three years to fund, on a matching basis with other donors, for activities to achieve a ban on landmines.
But the Soros Foundations' Landmines Project, to be based in Washington beginning in February, will not fund mine clearance or research and development "at this point," he said.

While the sums needed to undertake mine clearance dwarf the combined resources of private groups, he said, the situation was "altogether different" when it came to bringing about a ban on the production, export and use of landmines.

Mine clearing remains a painstaking, costly, dangerous job, largely involving removal by hand. But Israeli and South African experts have developed special demining vehicles, trained dogs and air-sampling devices to detect mines, Thomas McNamara, the assistant U.S. secretary of state for political-military affairs, told the conference.
President Bill Clinton has directed the Pentagon to develop new technology for use in the many countries still plagued by mines, including Bosnia, Cambodia, Angola and Mozambique, McNamara said.
